fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Devil As The Ultimate Boogeyman", "body": "Chance opens by pushing back on the wave of literalist Christianity moving through the truther scene, where Noah is a real man, the thousand year millennial reign has come and gone, and every problem gets blamed on Satan, Belial, Beelzebub, the Nephilim and the spirits of fallen angels. He argues this is the same product as the Gnostic prison planet, demiurge and simulation theory pitch. Every control system needs an ultimate boogeyman, because blame is what keeps people spending what he calls victim currency instead of taking responsibility for their own lives."}, {"title": "Original Sin And The Broken Self", "body": "The pair treat original sin as the load bearing lie of the whole structure. Chance describes it as convincing people they are intrinsically broken, that a tempter causes them to do bad things and that they have no real choice in the matter. Most people never say that out loud, but it is what the devil concept quietly installs in a culture. Dylan calls modern victimhood the cancer of society, noting how people now choose to be offended by a plain statement of preference, standards or a code of honor, and how coddling somebody in hard times helps nobody."}, {"title": "Language As Forensic Evidence Of Forgery", "body": "Dylan makes the case that scripture betrays itself through its own words. He asks why Paul would write to Romans in Greek to preach good news to Italians, comparing it to appealing to the British in Arabic. He points to terms like agion and agios carrying a martyrdom context alien to the Roman mind, arguing these passages cannot have been written when they are claimed to have been. Language is forensic, he says, because even a forgery leaves its fingerprints, and this is what exposes the third and fourth century takeover that severed the stories from nature."}, {"title": "Robert Taylor And The Beggarly Gospel", "body": "They continue their reading of Reverend Robert Taylor, a man they say was swept into the dustbin of history. The quoted passage calls the gospel peculiarly adapted for the poor, a beggarly gospel whose order of the day was to bring in the maimed, the halt and the blind and compel them to come in without ever asking their consent. Taylor calls it the morality necessary to keep the lower orders in subjection, and charges that those who thrive on it are too cowardly to defend it in open controversy against the infidels who challenge them."}, {"title": "Neutral Ground Between Creator And Destroyer", "body": "Both hosts insist this is not a Satanism pitch. Chance says they remain neutral, holding that everything scriptural is allegory for nature and the cycles created by the sun, so the symbolic identity of God and the devil is not an invitation to worship horns and a pitchfork. He traces the creator and destroyer schism to the Zoroastrian era and the split between Ahriman and his counterpart, and reads the devil's horns as the Hebrew qaran, radiance and light, the same rays and cornucopia symbolism found on old sculptures of Moses. Dylan adds that none of these Abrahamic systems are his culture."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Episode 6 of Inner Whirled continues our revival of the incredible Astronomico-Theological Lectures of the Rev. Robert Taylor, taking a deep dive into the details around the Devil in religious mythology. Our exploration encompasses the linguistic clues around this enigmatic figure, scriptural evidence for his true identity as an aspect of the Sun, how his titles and attributes mirror him to the savior archetype, what snakes have to do with it all, and much more. There's no better education out there to demystify the Devil, so bring your notebooks and enjoy!
